options.text: An asymptotic upper bound on the growth of a function
The memory address of the data
The exact running time in seconds

questions.explanation: Big-O bounds how fast a cost grows as input size increases, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. It abstracts away hardware speed to compare algorithms by scalability.

questions.prompt: Which growth rate is the fastest-growing (worst) among these?
questions.explanation: Exponential growth eventually dwarfs any polynomial, so O(2^n) is the worst here. The ordering from best to worst is log n, n log n, n^2, then 2^n.

questions.prompt: In Big-O analysis, the expression O(3n^2 + 5n + 100) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: Constant factors and lower-order terms are dropped, leaving the dominant term n^2. Only the fastest-growing part matters as n becomes large.

options.text: An asymptotic lower bound on growth
An asymptotic upper bound on growth

questions.explanation: Omega gives a lower bound — the cost grows at least this fast. When the upper and lower bounds match, Theta expresses the tight bound.

questions.prompt: A loop that runs from 1 to n, doubling a counter each iteration (1, 2, 4, 8, ...), executes how many times?
questions.explanation: The counter reaches n after about log2(n) doublings, so the loop is logarithmic. Halving each step gives the same count, which is why binary search is O(log n).

questions.prompt: Two nested loops, each running n times, give what time complexity?
questions.explanation: The inner loop runs n times for each of the n outer iterations, giving n x n = n^2 total steps. Nesting multiplies the counts.

options.text: The disk space of the operating system
The physical size of the source code
The extra memory an algorithm uses as a function of input size

questions.explanation: It counts the auxiliary memory beyond the input that scales with input size, such as recursion stacks and temporary arrays. An in-place algorithm uses O(1) auxiliary space.

questions.prompt: What is the recursion-stack space used by a balanced recursive traversal of a tree with n nodes?
questions.explanation: The stack depth equals the tree height, which is O(log n) when balanced. A skewed tree would push this to O(n).

questions.prompt: Why is worst-case complexity usually reported rather than best-case?

options.text: Best-case is undefined for most algorithms
It is always easier to compute
It reflects the fastest possible run
It gives a guarantee that holds for every input

questions.explanation: The worst case bounds performance no matter what input arrives, which is what a reliability-conscious engineer needs. Best-case can be misleadingly optimistic.

questions.prompt: What does amortised analysis capture that worst-case-per-operation does not?

options.text: The average cost per operation across a sequence, even if individual operations are occasionally expensive
The memory used by one operation

questions.explanation: Amortised analysis spreads the rare expensive operation, like a dynamic-array resize, across the many cheap ones. It shows appending is O(1) amortised despite an occasional O(n) resize.
